extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, and judges (readers of a treatise on patent transfer and licenses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on express licenses under patent law: who may grant them, territorial and temporal scope, how courts construe them, recording, effect of patent term extensions, estoppel, revocability, and related practical rules for licensors, licensees, assignees, purchasers and sublicensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may issue licenses; territorial scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Any owner of a patented invention may issue licenses in any form and to any extent he deems expedient. A patentee or assignee, whether sole or joint, may license for the whole or for any part of the United States. A grantee can license only within the territory covered by his ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license issued by one joint-owner is valid by estoppel against the other owners (though they may have an account for their share of the license-fee), but no part-owner can grant an exclusive license or otherwise restrict the licensing powers of the other owners. The licensee's rights can never exceed those of his licensor; the licensee must ascertain before purchase whether the licensor can convey the interest proposed (caveat emptor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive license is effectively an assignment (territory-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive license to make and use and sell operating upon the monopoly as well as the invention vests both in the licensee and, in reality though not in form, is an assignment or a grant according to the territory to which it relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat exclusive licenses of the whole territory as equivalent to assignments; parties should draft explicitly and consider consequences (e.g., recordation, rights on extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee rights limited to licensor's rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of the licensee can never exceed those of his licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any prior conveyance (assignment, grant, or license) limits the rights the licensee obtains; the licensee takes subject to limitations of earlier transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat emptor: licensee's duty to investigate licensor's title
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of caveat emptor is rigidly applied: it is the licensee's duty to ascertain before purchase whether the licensor has a good title to convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensees who fail to investigate cannot later claim broader rights than licensor had; courts will enforce that the licensee takes the interest subject to existing limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration: express license expires with original patent term unless otherwise agreed
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise agreed, an express license expires at the end of the original term of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the patentee or an assignee/grantee who has been conveyed the extended term can authorize practice during the extension; a license (even by those) is never presumed to cover the extended term unless such intention clearly and unequivocally appears on the face of the license itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: License coverage of patent extensions — presumption and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is presumed to cover only the original term of the patent; one who claims that it covers an extended term must prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts construe license language against coverage of extensions unless language is clear (cases cited: Hodge v. Hudson River, Pitts v. Hall, Clum v. Brewer indicating explicit language is required to include extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses may be drafted to endure through extensions if explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: A license may be made to endure under an extension, and the royalty will be collectible, if the instrument's language clearly embraces any subsequent extension of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties use language showing intent to cover extensions (e.g., 'for which letters-patent were or may be granted'), courts may hold the license covers the extended term (Clum v. Brewer, Case v. Redfield examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Congressional extension on licensee rights
rubrics_metrics.description: After an extension by act of Congress the licensee stands on his original title, not on the act of Congress granting the extension; the act protects but does not itself convey rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking a license under an extension admits the licensee has no rights other than those set out and may estop him from asserting otherwise (Union Mfg. Co. v. Lounsbury and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: license to a specific machine (instrument) vs. to make/sell
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is an instrument, a license to make it or to sell it expires with the original patent; but a license to use a particular instrument manufactured under the patent and duly sold remains in force, as to use, until the instrument is worn out and cannot be repaired without destroying identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law protects continued use/repair of tangible patented machines lawfully sold and in possession (right to repair and keep in employment until worn out). However, reconstruction or manufacturing new machines for use/sale after expiration generally requires a license under the extension; the saving clause applies only to machines embodied in tangible form (cases: Wetherell v. Passaic Zinc Co., Wood v. Michigan Southern, Hawley v. Mitchell).

rubrics_metrics.name: License to make/sell/construct expires with patent; right to repair/use of purchased items preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make, use, and sell machines for the term of the patent expires with the patent; the purchaser of the implement acquires title to the implement but not a portion of the franchise; he may use and repair machines purchased until worn out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete title to the purchased implement vests in the vendee; that title does not convey the monopoly franchise. The assignee/ grantee's right to use during extension applies only to machines that passed lawfully out of the monopoly by sale during the original term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process/art licenses — uncertain treatment; may continue through extension if granted by patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to use an art (process) analogously should terminate with the original patent, but courts have held where such a license is granted by the patentee (or by an assignee to whom the extension has been conveyed) it may continue during the extended term and authorize procurement of new apparatus after extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal conflicts exist; licensees may waive various rights by taking new licenses from owners of extended term. Cases cited: Day v. Union India Rubber Co., and others — careful drafting recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal licenses terminate on licensee's death unless assigns included
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to a specific person ceases at his death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a license is personal and unassignable, articles on hand at death may be sold by representatives in some cases; but generally personal licenses do not survive absent assignment language (cases: Oliver v. Rumford Chemical Works, Montross v. Mabie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses are not recordable and record is not constructive notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is not such a conveyance of an interest as to affect ownership and hence is not required to be recorded. The record of a license, not being legally required, is not constructive notice to any person or for any purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent purchasers take title subject to rights of existing irrevocable licensees, but they bear the risk of informing themselves. Irrevocable licenses (even if unrecorded) are good against subsequent purchasers; however, recordation does not give constructive notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts construe licenses by the parties' intention; parol evidence and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is construed by the courts according to the intention of the parties as manifested by the language they employ. If the license is in writing all previous parol agreements concerning the same subject are merged; oral evidence is not admissible to expand, contract, or vary its provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When several licenses/contracts constitute one transaction they are to be considered together. Practical construction (course of conduct) may be considered if not inconsistent with the instrument. Scope of a general license is limited by the patent on which it is based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions precedent and suspension of privileges for nonperformance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a parol agreement was a condition precedent to the license, the condition must be performed before the privileges vest; any premature exercise of them is infringement and will render the licensee liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation of concurrent license conditions suspends privileges and subjects the licensee to breach of contract suits or injunctions; a licensee persisting after repudiation may be sued as an infringer and cannot plead the license as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocability: unconditional/gross-paid licenses vs revocable licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a license is not made irrevocable by its terms, or not paid for by a gross sum in advance, the licensor may recall it on condition broken; an unconditional license limited in duration by the life of the patent is irrevocable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to the terms and consideration; licenses paid for by a lump sum or expressly made unconditional are treated as irrevocable; otherwise the licensor may rescind on breach of condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel: licensee exercising licensed privileges is estopped from denying patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee, having accepted a license and while exercising thereunder the rights conferred, is estopped from denying the validity of the patent in any suit where such exercise of license privileges is the basis of the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions and nuances: a purchaser from the licensee is not necessarily estopped; a licensee who repudiates the license may thereafter challenge validity for future use; suits to recover license fees tied to quantity made generally bar denial of validity; courts distinguish contexts (royalties, completed sales, actions for license-fees). See cases: Consolidated Middlings Purifier Co., Brown v. Lapham, Wilder v. ? and others cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repudiation: licensee may repudiate and then challenge validity for future use but not avoid past royalties on completed sales
rubrics_metrics.description: If the licensee repudiates the license (ceases to claim its protection), as to his future exercise of privileges he may defend on the ground the patent is invalid; after such repudiation he may also dispute validity in actions against him for license fees for the past making or use of the invention, but not for royalties on completed sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a license expressly admits patent validity and precludes impairment of that admission, the licensee cannot attack validity during the term. Repudiation changes estoppel posture — careful transactional drafting advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublicenses and agent-made licenses: expiration and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A sublicense to practise an invention expires with the term of the patent. Where an agent of the patentee, for valuable consideration, licenses another to construct a device embodying the invention, the patentee has no right to the device, but the licensee may use the invention in connection with such device (subject to extension rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublicenses do not extend beyond the original patent term unless instrument plainly so provides. Agent-made licenses can create rights in licensee but do not expand patentee's rights in the agent's device; drafting clarity about scope and territory is essential.
